name: The Khmer Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Khmer Empire: From God-King to Slave
period: 1181–1297 (from Jayavarman VII to Zhou Daguan's stay at Angkor)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You are hailed as a god-king, and the temple at the heart of your city celebrates your divine rule; but princes of your own house have often seized the throne by force, and one of them may seize it from you.
tiers.kid: The kings of Angkor were seen as gods on earth, and they built huge stone temples such as Angkor Wat and the Bayon.
tiers.rise: No settled rule governed the succession: of the 27 rulers of Kambuja, eleven lacked a legitimate claim to power. Suryavarman I took the throne by seizing Angkor, Jayavarman VII by retaking it from the Cham, and in 1295 Jayavarman VIII was deposed by his son-in-law Srindravarman.
tiers.why: Since Jayavarman II proclaimed himself chakravartin, “universal ruler”, and devaraja, “god-king”, in 802, Khmer kings were held to have the divine quality of living gods, incarnations of Shiva or Vishnu.

tiers.name: Royalty, ministers and nobles
tiers.you: You ride behind the king on an elephant under a red umbrella, and your house, larger than any commoner’s, has a tiled roof over its family temple; but in the next struggle for the throne you must choose your prince well.
tiers.kid: Princes and ministers rode on elephants under red umbrellas, and the higher a man’s rank, the bigger his house.
tiers.rise: Royal and noble birth gave entry to the rank, but its members fought over it: Khmer kings and royal families were often caught up in power struggles over the succession or rivalries over principalities, and the relationship between the rulers and their elites was unstable. A prince could rise as a soldier, as Jayavarman VII did, leading armies under earlier kings before he took the throne.
tiers.why: The kshatriyas, royalty, nobles, warlords, soldiers and warriors, formed the governing elite.

tiers.name: Brahmins
tiers.you: You are a Brahmin of the court, performing the Hindu rites of the king and his nobles, and you may also hold high office in his service.
tiers.kid: Brahmins were Hindu priests who led the ceremonies of the king and the nobles.
tiers.rise: The priests’ fortunes followed the king’s faith. Jayavarman VII made Mahayana Buddhism the state religion and had Hindu temples altered to show the Buddha; from about 1243 Jayavarman VIII restored Hinduism, made the Bayon a temple to Shiva and replaced Buddha images with lingams. From the 14th century Theravada Buddhism prevailed, and the last Sanskrit inscription dates from 1327.
tiers.why: Hinduism was the state religion for most of the empire’s history, and its ceremonies and rituals were performed by Brahmins, usually only among the king’s family, the nobles and the ruling class.

tiers.name: Buddhist monks
tiers.you: You have shaved your head and put on the yellow robe of a Theravada monk; your temple is plain, and its Buddha images are made of gilded plaster.
tiers.kid: Buddhist monks at Angkor shaved their heads and wore yellow robes.
tiers.rise: The surviving sources say little of how men entered or left the monkhood. The faith’s spread mattered to the whole order: George Coedès argued that Theravada’s denial of the ultimate reality of the individual sapped the royal cult that had raised the great temples.
tiers.why: For most of the Angkor period Buddhism came after Hinduism in popularity, though kings built Buddhist temples and monasteries beside their Hindu shrines, and Jayavarman VII founded Ta Prohm for his mother and Preah…

tiers.name: Traders and artisans
tiers.you: You sit on a straw mat in the open market of Angkor selling your wares for rice, cloth or Chinese coins, and you pay an official rent for your patch of ground.
tiers.kid: At Angkor’s market most of the traders were women, who sat on straw mats on the ground to sell their goods.
tiers.rise: Newcomers brought crafts of their own: settlers from Siam grew mulberry trees, raised silkworms and wove silk, and the local people asked Siamese women to mend their clothes. A Chinese man arriving at Angkor, Zhou wrote, first took in a local woman, partly to profit from her skill in trade.
tiers.why: Among the other classes were traders and artisans: carpenters and stonemasons, potters, metalworkers, goldsmiths and textile weavers.

tiers.name: Rice farmers and fishermen
tiers.you: You live in a bamboo house on stilts by your rice fields, with your pigs and hens beneath the floor, and eat rice and fish paste; when the Siamese come, you are sent to face them with a lance and a shield.
tiers.kid: Most Khmer people were rice farmers and fishermen who lived in bamboo houses on stilts, safe from floods.
tiers.rise: War reached them all: when the Siamese attacked, Zhou wrote, ordinary people were ordered to face them without strategy or preparation, and soldiers fought naked and barefoot with lance and shield. When droughts and floods damaged the waterworks in the 14th and 15th centuries, many may have left the great cities and moved south.
tiers.why: Rice farmers and fishermen formed the large majority.

tiers.name: Temple servants
tiers.you: You are one of the 12,640 people who serve the temple of Ta Prohm, and the rice that feeds you is grown by a great host of farmers.
tiers.kid: Giant temples like Ta Prohm needed thousands of people to look after them.
tiers.rise: The surviving sources used here do not say how people came to serve a temple, or whether they could leave. George Coedès argued that the spread of Theravada Buddhism wore away the royal cult that had raised the temples, and the workforce that served them may have shrunk with it.
tiers.why: Only the gods had a right to houses of stone, so the temples were the empire’s great buildings, and they needed a great workforce.

tiers.name: Slaves
tiers.you: You are a slave, on the lowest rung of Khmer society, beneath the farmers and fishermen.
tiers.kid: At the bottom of Khmer society were slaves, people who belonged to others and were not free.
tiers.rise: How people became slaves at Angkor, and whether they could go free, is not recorded in the sources used here.
tiers.why: Slaves stood on the lowest social level of Khmer society, beneath the farmers and fishermen.
